title: Limit points, derived set, closure, and density
section: Point-Set Topology ▷ The Interior, Exterior, Boundary, Limit Points, and Closure of a Set
terms: limit point; accumulation point; cluster point; derived set; closure; isolated point; dense subset.

exposition.text:
′
A limit point of A is a point whose every neighborhood meets A \ {x}; the derived set A consists
of all such points. The closure A consists of points whose every neighborhood meets A, so A =
′
A ∪ A . It is the smallest closed set containing A.
A point x ∈ A is isolated if some neighborhood N satisfies N ∩ A = {x}. Such a point belongs
to the closure but is not a limit point. A subset is dense in X if its closure equals X. In metric
spaces, points of the closure are limits of sequences in A; this sequential characterization should
not be assumed for arbitrary topologies.

solution.text:
′
The only accumulation points are 0 and 2, so A = {0, 2}. A finite subset of the real line
has no accumulation points; its derived set is empty.

question.text:
Let A = Q ∩ (0, 1) and B = (R \ Q) ∩ (0, 1). Which equality is correct?
(A) A ∩ B = A ∩ B (B) A ∩ B = [0, 1]
′
(C) A ∪ B = (0, 1) (D) A = ∅
(E) int(A ∪ B) = ∅

solution.text:
Both A and B are dense in (0, 1) and accumulate at its endpoints, so their closures are
[0, 1]. Their intersection is empty, showing why closure need not commute with intersec-
tions. Their union is (0, 1).

question.text:
Let A = {1/n + 1/m : n, m ∈ N}. What is the set of limit points of its derived set?
(A) Q ∩ [0, 2] (B) {1/n : n ∈ N} (C) ∅ (D) {0} (E) [0, 2]

solution.text:
The derived set is {0} ∪ {1/n : n ≥ 1}. Each 1/n is approached by holding n fixed and
letting m → ∞; zero is approached by n = m → ∞. Conversely, take a convergent se-
quence of distinct values 1/n + 1/m. If both indices tend to infinity along a subsequence, its
limit is zero. Otherwise some index has a fixed value along a subsequence; distinctness then
forces a further subsequence of the other index to tend to infinity, giving limit 1/n or 1/m.
These exhaust possible limits. This derived set has only zero as an accumulation point, so
its derived set is {0}.

question.text:
For any subset A of a metric space, which equality always holds?
(A) A = A (B) A is open (C) A = A (D) int A = int A (E) A ∩ B = A ∩ B for every B

solution.text:
Closure is closed, so taking its closure adds no points. The other assertions fail, for exam-
ple using disjoint dense sets or nonclosed subsets.

question.text:
If A and B are dense open subsets of R, which must be true?
(A) A ∩ B = R (B) A \ B is empty (C) A ∩ B is dense (D) A ∩ B is closed (E) A = B

solution.text:
Any nonempty open interval meets A in a nonempty open set. Density of B makes that set
meet B as well, proving the intersection meets every open interval.
